title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation

paper.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity
field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an
analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical
relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a
relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global
gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first,
sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential — but
obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once
per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear
injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer
carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small
injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained
by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by
relaxation alone, matching the original model’s FID to within 0.04 0.04 at
CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without
backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation’s
parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998 0.9998 , and training end to end
with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10
generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at
competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not
require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions
and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern generative models are expensive to train ( Strubell et al., 2019 ) and expensive to sample ( Luccioni et al., 2024 ) : diffusion, flow matching and related methods typically produce one image by integrating a velocity field over hundreds of sequential steps, each a full pass through a large network. Sequential work of this kind suits a GPU poorly and a physical system well. A substrate that relaxes to the minimum of an energy performs in one continuous settling what a GPU performs as hundreds of discrete evaluations, and analog neuromorphic devices promise large gains in speed and energy on that basis. Two things stand in the way: finding a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and removing the backpropagation that training relies on. Energy Matching ( Balcerak et al., 2025 ) is one such algorithm. It generates by gradient descent on a potential V θ ​ ( x ) V_{\theta}(x) , the scalar output of a feedforward network, whose minima are where the data lies. The potential does not change with time, so every step descends the same fixed landscape, which is what a physical system does when it relaxes. But the velocity it follows is − ∇ x V θ -\nabla_{x}V_{\theta} , and in its original formulation obtaining that gradient is a backward pass — once per integration step during sampling, on top of the usual ∇ θ ℒ \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L} backward pass per training step. The remaining obstacle is therefore backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is difficult to realise in analog. Mixed-signal crossbar designs convert between analog and digital at every layer, at a cost in energy and latency ( Kendall et al., 2020 ) . Physics-aware training instead runs the forward pass physically but the backward pass through a digital model of the substrate, and pays for digital computation at every training step ( Wright et al., 2022 ) . Both pay a digital cost the physics does not.

sections.heading: Generation without a backward pass.
sections.text: An Energy Matching model trained conventionally by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation, so that a substrate hosting it needs no backward pass anywhere in the generation path. At CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale the velocities agree with autograd’s to a cosine similarity of 1 1 to nine decimal places, and the FID of the generated samples matches to within 0.04 0.04 (Section 4.1 ). No retraining is required, so the energy and latency of generation — most of a deployed model’s lifetime cost — could be cut on analog hardware without any change to how the model is trained.

sections.heading: Training without a backward pass.
sections.text: Training can move on-chip as well. The PCN relaxes on an explicit energy, so it can be trained by Equilibrium Propagation ( Scellier and Bengio, 2017 ) , which reads parameter updates − ∇ θ ℒ -\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L} from local measurements at equilibrium and so needs none of the global transport that makes backpropagation awkward in analog. We use the GradEP variant ( Gower, 2026 ) , which trains gradients of energy landscapes — here the velocities Energy Matching generates with. We call the resulting procedure PotentialEP . Its parameter updates reproduce backpropagation’s to a cosine similarity of 0.9998 0.9998 at our operating point (Section 4.2 ), and a model trained end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10, against 3.54 3.54 for backpropagation (Section 5 ). To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule.

sections.heading: The architecture.
sections.text: A backpropagation-free algorithm is of little use if the architecture it trains is itself hard to realise in analog, and two components of the one we inherit from Energy Matching are: group normalisation, which couples every channel through a shared statistic, and attention, whose pairwise products are not a fixed weighted sum. We find that removing both costs nothing measurable at this scale — a network of only convolutions, pointwise nonlinearities and UNet skips, every operation of the kind an analog crossbar performs natively, reaches a CIFAR-10 FID of 3.51 3.51 (Section 5.1 ).

sections.text: A predictive coding network ( Rao and Ballard, 1999 ; Whittington and Bogacz, 2017 ) assigns a dynamical variable h k h_{k} to each node of a feedforward architecture and an energy to the mismatch between each node and the prediction made of it by its predecessor: E = ∑ k = 1 N 1 2 ​ ‖ f k ​ ( h k − 1 ) − h k ‖ 2 , e k = f k ​ ( h k − 1 ) − h k . E=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\tfrac{1}{2}\big\|f_{k}(h_{k-1})-h_{k}\big\|^{2},\qquad e_{k}=f_{k}(h_{k-1})-h_{k}. (4) Inference is not a forward pass but a relaxation: with the input h 0 = x h_{0}=x clamped, the states descend E E to a stationary point, and outputs are read from the settled state. Two properties of that stationary state are what Section 3.1 builds on. First, with only error terms present the minimum is e = 0 e=0 , which by induction from h 0 = x h_{0}=x is exactly the forward pass: left to itself the relaxation reproduces the feedforward network it was built from. sections.heading: 2.3 Equilibrium Propagation
sections.text: Equilibrium Propagation ( Scellier and Bengio, 2017 ; Laborieux et al., 2020 ) is an alternative learning algorithm to backpropagation for systems whose dynamics settle to stationary points, from which their outputs are read. It uses only local measurements at equilibrium, making it a natural candidate for neuromorphic hardware. Consider a system with state s s , parameters θ \theta and energy E ⁡ ( s , θ ) E(s;\theta) , relaxing to an equilibrium s ∗ s^{*} whose position we want to train so that the outputs reduce a cost C ⁡ ( s ) C(s) . Adding β ​ C ​ ( s ) \beta C(s) to the energy displaces that equilibrium towards lower cost, and the parameter gradient can be read from where and how far it moves. Each training sample therefore takes three phases: a free phase relaxing to s ∗ s^{*} , then two nudged phases relaxing E ± β ​ C E\pm\beta C to s ∗ ± β s^{*\pm\beta} , at lower and higher cost respectively. The update is Δ ​ θ ∝ − 1 2 ​ β ​ [ ∂ E ∂ θ | s ∗ + β − ∂ E ∂ θ | s ∗ − β ] → β → 0 − ∇ θ C ​ ( s ∗ ) , \Delta\theta\;\propto\;-\frac{1}{2\beta}\Big[\frac{\partial E}{\partial\theta}\Big|_{s^{*+\beta}}-\frac{\partial E}{\partial\theta}\Big|_{s^{*-\beta}}\Big]\;\xrightarrow[\beta\to 0]{}\;-\nabla_{\theta}\,C(s^{*}), (5) which lowers the energy at s ∗ + β s^{*+\beta} and raises it at s ∗ − β s^{*-\beta} , so that the free equilibrium s ∗ s^{*} itself shifts towards lower cost. For small enough β \beta this is exactly gradient descent on C ⁡ ( s ∗ ) C(s^{*}) . Each ∂ E / ∂ θ \partial E/\partial\theta is a local quantity — on a PCN, e k ⊤ ​ ∂ f k / ∂ θ k e_{k}^{\top}\partial f_{k}/\partial\theta_{k} — so the whole procedure runs without global backward passes. EP has been scaled to CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification, including on PCN energies ( Kerjan et al., 2026 ) , but its generative applications remain at MNIST scale and below ( Meersch et al., 2023 ; Gower, 2026 ) . The cost C C must be a function of s ∗ s^{*} itself, the position the state settles at, since that is what the nudge displaces. A loss involving an energy gradient at that position — such as Energy Matching’s equation 2 involving ∇ x V \nabla_{x}V — is therefore out of reach. GradEP ( Gower, 2026 ) resolves this by running EP on a modified energy whose equilibrium position encodes the gradient of the original energy, so that moving the former’s equilibrium trains the latter’s gradient. Section 3.2 applies this to the PCN of Section 3.1 , and Section 3.2.1 improves the nudge it uses.

sections.text: We now ask what training on the PCN requires, comparing the updates it produces — by EP, Δ ​ θ EP \Delta\theta_{\rm EP} , and by the implicit-function solve of Section 3.2 , Δ ​ θ IFT \Delta\theta_{\rm IFT} — against the backpropagation gradient Δ ​ θ BP \Delta\theta_{\rm BP} of the same feedforward model on the same batch. sections.heading: The correspondence itself is not the constraint.
sections.text: Where EP estimates the parameter gradient by a finite difference of two nudged equilibria, the implicit solve obtains it directly at equilibrium, so its only error is the O ⁡ ( γ ) O(\gamma) correspondence bias of Section 4.1 . Even in TF32 cos ⁡ ( Δ ​ θ IFT , Δ ​ θ BP ) \cos(\Delta\theta_{\rm IFT},\Delta\theta_{\rm BP}) is exact to four decimal places from γ = 10 − 7 \gamma=10^{-7} to 10 − 2 10^{-2} , softening only to 0.998 0.998 at γ = 10 − 1 \gamma=10^{-1} , and is equally insensitive to the number of conjugate-gradient steps (App. H ). Everything that follows is therefore a test of EP’s finite-difference estimator rather than of the correspondence.

sections.heading: 5 CIFAR-10 generation by backprop-free training
sections.text: The previous section established both correspondences at fixed weights. We now train with them end to end, over 10 5 10^{5} steps, and measure the generation quality of the resulting model. We train three arms: the feedforward Energy Matching model by backpropagation, and the PCN at γ = 10 − 4 \gamma=10^{-4} by the implicit solve and by EP with the linearised nudge. The architecture, optimiser, schedule, batch size, EMA decay and step budget are shared; initialisation and the random draws of training are not. The EP arm’s phase-2 differs further: a smaller γ \gamma , a stiffer tether λ \lambda and a larger β \beta , starting from its 100 100 k phase-1 checkpoint rather than 145 145 k. Relaxation settings are in Table 6 and the rest of the recipe in App. J .

sections.heading: 5.1 Hardware-plausible architectures
sections.text: PotentialEP is neuromorphically compatible as an algorithm, but the energy it trains is only as neuromorphically implementable as the architecture defining it. Two components we inherit from Energy Matching are not easily realised on an analog substrate: group normalisation, which couples every channel at a layer through a shared statistic, and attention, whose pairwise products are not a fixed weighted sum. We therefore ask how much generation quality is lost when both are removed. Replacing them with weight standardisation, which normalises each filter’s weights rather than its activations, residual scaling by 1 / depth 1/\sqrt{\text{depth}} , and a flat linear head in place of the ViT (App. I ) leaves an architecture with no operation beyond fixed weighted sums and pointwise nonlinearities — both native to analog crossbar hardware, the sums through Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws ( Ielmini and Wong, 2018 ; Sebastian et al., 2020 ) . We train this arm by backpropagation, our compute budget not extending to a second full EP run, and it reaches an FID of 3.51 3.51 against the full architecture’s 3.54 3.54 : the two are indistinguishable at the resolution of the measurement. Generation competitive with the diffusion and flow-matching baselines of Table 2 therefore does not require either component. This architecture is wider ( 78 78 M against 50 50 M) and used a different schedule and a longer first phase (App. I ), so we take it as an existence proof and leave a cheaper recipe to future work.

sections.heading: Predictive coding.
sections.text: Generative predictive coding typically places the image at the bottom of a hierarchy of predictions: Monte Carlo predictive coding samples it by adding Langevin noise to inference, at MNIST scale ( Oliviers et al., 2024 ) , and Langevin predictive coding samples a latent code the same way and decodes it, reaching CIFAR-10 at FID 113 113 ( Zahid et al., 2023 ) . In both, the image is the predicted layer of a prediction-error likelihood. In ours it is the input of a network whose scalar output is an explicit potential, and the force on it is that potential’s gradient.

sections.heading: Generation by energy descent.
sections.text: Energy Matching ( Balcerak et al., 2025 ) , which we build on, generates by descent on an explicit scalar potential. Equilibrium Matching ( Wang and Du, 2025 ) learns a time-invariant gradient field, in its best-performing form without an explicit energy, and Rodriguez et al. (2026) train it on an Energy Transformer, whose blocks relax latent tokens on a Hopfield-type energy, reaching class-conditional FID 28.56 28.56 on CIFAR-10. There the image-space update is a learned function of the relaxed tokens rather than the gradient of any energy in x x ; in ours it is the gradient of γ − 1 ​ E PCN = V θ + O ⁡ ( γ ) \gamma^{-1}E_{\rm PCN}=V_{\theta}+O(\gamma) . Each of these works trains by backpropagation.

sections.heading: Physical and neuromorphic generation.
sections.text: A parallel line generates with physical substrates. Simulated Kuramoto oscillators ( Unconventional AI, 2026 ) and continuous spins descending a learned quadratic energy ( Sun et al., 2026 ) evolve a latent state from a random start and render it through a small convolutional decoder, reaching class-conditional CIFAR-10 FID 8.76 8.76 and clean-FID 9.71 9.71 respectively, the former also at ImageNet 64 × 64 64\times 64 . Optical systems have implemented a diffusion model’s denoiser ( Oguz et al., 2024 ) and a single-pass generator ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , demonstrated in hardware at MNIST scale, and spiking diffusion models target event-driven neuromorphic chips ( Cao et al., 2024 ) . All of these are trained by backpropagation. Bösch et al. (2026) generate 28 × 28 28\times 28 MNIST zeros and ones with a local rule, on an energy with no hidden units. Ours relaxes in image space with no decoder, and uses Equilibrium Propagation to obtain local updates for an energy with hidden layers.

sections.heading: Simulation cost.
sections.text: On a GPU, an EP training step costs about sixteen times a backpropagation step, and an implicit-solve step about five, with the relaxation budgets dominating. A substrate that settles physically would not pay that cost, but its speed, energy and settling accuracy remain unmeasured: everything here is simulated.

sections.heading: Locality and hardware realisation.
sections.text: The relaxation is local in the sense EP requires: every quantity a weight update needs is present at its two ends. The nodes of our training runs are, however, architecture blocks rather than single weight matrices, chosen to reduce simulation cost, so a literal implementation would need circuitry to carry the error through each block’s internal layers. One node per weight matrix removes this, and left the training gradient unchanged in the one checkpoint we measured (App. D ). Analog EP also obtains the backward drive J ⊤ ​ e J^{\top}e from a feedback pathway programmed to match the forward one; any drift between the two leaves dynamics that descend no energy at all ( Kendall et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: Scope of the evidence.
sections.text: App. K collects the scope of each claim. Each arm is a single run, so training variance is unknown, and the small FID differences do not establish a ranking. We demonstrate EP training on CIFAR-10 only; at ImageNet-32 we verify the inference correspondence on the authors’ released checkpoints, but did not train. The hardware-plausible architecture was trained and sampled only as a feedforward network, so it has not been demonstrated together with EP. The equilibria were computed by noise-free digital relaxation in error coordinates; the local state dynamics share their fixed points (App. E ) but were not run to equilibrium at this scale. Analog noise, finite bit depth and forward–backward pathway mismatch remain untested.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We used a frontier large language model in three ways. For the paper’s prose, we used it iteratively at the sentence level — for wording, concision and clarity — rather than to draft sections or generate content; the ideas, claims and structure are the author’s. For the code, we used it to help write and debug the training, sampling and measurement implementations; every suggestion was read and accepted or rejected manually, and the numerical results reported here come from runs of the accepted code. For related work, we used it to expand a literature search the author had already conducted; we checked every claim we attribute to a cited work against that work directly. We did not use it to generate research ideas or hypotheses, to analyse results, or to produce figures. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this paper, including its text, claims and artifacts.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The PCN construction and the correspondence it rests on are given in Section 3.1 , with the full derivation, its assumptions and the order of every neglected term in App. A ; the extension to the skip-connected UNet is in App. D and the solver we relax with in App. E . sections.text: The linearisation does not depend on the form of E PCN E_{\rm PCN} , so it applies to any use of GradEP with a quadratic loss. The UNet we adopt is not a chain: its decoder blocks consume a concatenation of their predecessor and a topologically distant encoder state, so a node may have several parents, and an encoder node several children. sections.heading: D.4 The adopted graph
sections.text: For the runs of the main text we use block granularity, so that whole modules of the backbone serve as f k f_{k} unmodified. The graph has N = 27 N=27 nodes: twelve encoder blocks chained from the input, the middle block, twelve decoder blocks each taking [ previous , skip ] [\text{previous},\text{skip}] as parents with the skip popped from the encoder stack in the architecture’s own order, the output projection, and the ViT head producing o o . The time-conditioning pathway inherited from the diffusion backbone is not a node: V ⁡ ( x ) V(x) is time-independent, so it receives a fixed constant, which each block sees as a trained per-channel bias. 2 2 2 The feedforward reference does the same; injecting the identical constant is what preserves exact agreement with its forward pass. The pathway carries no state and does not relax.

sections.heading: The state parameterisation is impractically slow.
sections.text: At d ​ t = 1 \mathrm{d}t=1 the state relaxation diverges within a few sweeps, in float64 as in float32, so the failure is a dynamical instability rather than a precision floor. Below the stability bound it does converge, monotonically and to the same fixed point as the error relaxation, as a shared stationary point requires. But it converges at a measured rate implying a condition number of about 2 × 10 7 2\times 10^{7} : at d ​ t = 2 × 10 − 5 \mathrm{d}t=2\times 10^{-5} , reaching equilibrium takes of the order of 10 8 10^{8} sweeps, against one in error coordinates. This cost is a property of the explicit discretisation rather than of the dynamics: a continuous system settles at the rate of its slowest mode, not its fastest, and Goemaere et al. (2026, App. B.5) make the same point, that the decay which makes discrete state updates slow is an artefact of time discretisation.

sections.text: The error parameterisation is therefore not just a convenience but what makes the relaxation of this network practical. Three further properties follow from its near-identity Hessian, each measured elsewhere in the paper. The relaxation reaches equilibrium in a single deadbeat sweep from feedforward initialisation (App. F ). The implicit-gradient solve of Section 3.2 inverts a matrix already close to the identity, so one conjugate-gradient step is as accurate as fifty (App. H ). Finally, float32 suffices: at the operating γ \gamma the velocity’s deviation from autograd’s sits below the arithmetic’s own floor (Section 4.1 ). Part of the reason is that the error parameterisation never forms an error as the difference of two nearly equal states, which in state coordinates costs significant digits of precision in every error.

sections.heading: Appendix I The hardware-plausible architecture
sections.text: This appendix specifies the norm- and attention-free architecture of Section 5.1 in enough detail to reimplement, together with the training recipe it needed. It shows only that competitive generation is possible on an architecture an analog substrate could run, not that this particular architecture is the optimal one. We give our reasons for the individual choices where we have them, but which of them are necessary, and at what cost, we leave to future work.

sections.heading: What was removed and what replaced it.
sections.text: The architecture is built from the Energy Matching UNet but with three changes. Firstly, all 51 51 group-normalisation layers are replaced by the identity. Secondly, all 6 6 attention blocks are replaced by the identity, which must be done on the built module tree rather than by configuration: the UNet’s middle block hardcodes ResBlock–Attention–ResBlock, so setting the attention resolutions alone cannot produce an attention-free network. Thirdly, the ViT head is replaced by a flat one, which flattens the UNet’s 3 × 32 × 32 3\times 32\times 32 output and applies Linear ⁡ ( 3072,512 ) \mathrm{Linear}(3072,512) , SiLU, Linear ⁡ ( 512 , 1 ) \mathrm{Linear}(512,1) . We re-initialise the UNet’s final convolution from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.02 ) \mathcal{N}(0,0.02) rather than leaving it at the flow-matching codebase’s zero initialisation, after an earlier variant of the head failed to train from zero. We did not test whether the flat head trains without this. Two further changes are made to the remaining convolutions and residual blocks. Firstly, weight standardisation ( Qiao et al., 2020 ) replaces each convolution’s weights by w ^ i = g i ​ w i σ i ​ fan ​ - ​ in + ϵ , σ i = std ⁡ ( w i ) , \hat{w}_{i}=\frac{g_{i}\,w_{i}}{\sigma_{i}\sqrt{\mathrm{fan\text{-}in}}+\epsilon},\qquad\sigma_{i}=\operatorname{std}(w_{i}), (41) per output filter i i , with g i g_{i} a learned per-filter gain initialised to σ i ​ fan ​ - ​ in \sigma_{i}\sqrt{\mathrm{fan\text{-}in}} so that the reparameterisation is exactly the identity at initialisation. No mean subtraction is applied. It is applied to every convolution except the zero-initialised ones — therefore 42 42 convolutions are standardised and 23 23 are left plain on the built model. Those 23 23 are each ResBlock’s second convolution, zero-initialised by the flow-matching codebase so that every block starts as the identity; standardising an all-zero filter would leave both its weight and gain gradients at zero, so it could never leave that initialisation. Secondly, residual scaling replaces each ResBlock’s output by skip + ρ ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( x ) − skip ) \mathrm{skip}+\rho\,(f(x)-\mathrm{skip}) with ρ = 1 / 22 = 0.213 \rho=1/\sqrt{22}=0.213 , one over the square root of the number of ResBlocks ( De and Smith, 2020 ) . Neither requires computation at inference: w ^ \hat{w} depends only on the weights, so a crossbar is programmed with it once and never recomputes a normalisation at runtime, and ρ \rho is a wiring gain. The resolution-changing path needed no modification: downsampling is a stride- 2 2 convolution rather than pooling, upsampling is nearest-neighbour interpolation followed by a stride- 1 1 convolution, and both are weighted sums like any other convolution.

sections.heading: Module census.
sections.text: The built model contains 42 42 standardised convolutions, 23 23 plain convolutions, 22 22 ResBlocks, 26 26 linear layers, 69 69 SiLU activations, and zero group-normalisation, attention or layer-normalisation modules, against 51 51 , 14 14 and 16 16 of those respectively in the architecture it replaces. It carries 78.4 78.4 M parameters against 50.0 50.0 M, from the flat head’s 3072 × 512 3072\times 512 first linear layer and a base channel width of 192 192 against 128 128 , which widens every stage through the same multipliers.

sections.heading: How we arrived at this configuration.
sections.text: We reached it by trial rather than by systematic search. Attention and the ViT head could each be removed without much cost, but removing normalisation made training diverge, and weight standardisation was what made the fully stripped network trainable. We did not establish which ingredients are necessary, at what width, or under what schedule; that investigation is left to future work.

sections.heading: Training recipe.
sections.text: This arm is trained by backpropagation, with the settings of Table 6 . It differs from the other arms by using a cosine learning rate schedule, annealing to zero at 145 145 k steps, then a constant learning rate of 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} from 145 145 k to 175 175 k steps, after which the second phase is conducted as usual. We arrived at this change by trial after a constant learning rate of 1.2 × 10 − 3 1.2\times 10^{-3} destabilised partway through the first phase; we did not try a lower constant rate from scratch, and the successful run spent most of its life below 10 − 3 10^{-3} , so the schedule rather than the annealing may be what mattered.

sections.heading: Sampling time.
sections.text: The contrastive phase shifts the optimal sampling time in both architectures, and further in this one. Sampled on a common τ s \tau_{s} ladder after that phase, the full architecture (under all three training rules) is best at τ s = 3.25 \tau_{s}=3.25 and this one at τ s = 5.0 \tau_{s}=5.0 , and both are much worse at τ s = 1 \tau_{s}=1 than before the contrastive phase. Phase 2 optimises the potential for the Langevin regime at the expense of the noiseless endpoint, and this architecture is affected more.

sections.heading: Appendix J Experimental implementation
sections.text: This appendix gives the settings needed to reproduce the runs of Section 5 , and the implementation choices that the PCN formulation requires but a feedforward one does not. Code is available at https://github.com/alexgower/EnergyMatchingEqProp .

sections.heading: Shared recipe.
sections.text: Table 6 gives the settings shared by all arms, and the relaxation settings of the two PCN arms. The three arms of Section 5 share the architecture, optimiser, learning rate, schedule, effective batch size, EMA decay, step budget and data pipeline; the norm- and attention-free arm differs as App. I describes. What they do not share is the random realisation: there is no global seed in the trainer, so each arm has its own initialisation, its own noise samples for the optimal-transport coupling and the contrastive negatives, and its own dropout masks. With one run per arm we have no estimate of run-to-run variance, and the differences in Table 2 should be read with that in mind. The implicit-solve arm holds x x fixed at x t x_{t} and differentiates the flow loss on v PCN ​ ( x t ) v_{\rm PCN}(x_{t}) with respect to θ \theta , using the implicit function theorem for the dependence of h ∗ h^{*} on θ \theta , so it uses no tether; the tethered objective ℒ PCN \mathcal{L}_{\rm PCN} approaches this fixed- x x one as γ / λ → 0 \gamma/\lambda\to 0 (App. B ).

sections.heading: Asynchronous relaxation.
sections.text: Nodes are updated in even/odd sweeps ( Kerjan et al., 2026 ) , the second half-step seeing the first’s updated values, so one sweep costs two energy evaluations. On a chain this is exactly Gauss–Seidel, since same-parity nodes share no energy term; on the DAG of App. D a skip may connect two same-parity nodes, so the decoupling is only approximate. We adopt it because Kerjan et al. (2026) find synchronous updates substantially worse at the same step size, and sometimes divergent; we did not repeat that comparison here. The fixed point is the same either way.

sections.heading: Frozen dropout.
sections.text: A PCN training step evaluates the network many times: T free T_{\rm free} sweeps during the free phase and T nudge T_{\rm nudge} in each nudged phase, each with K h K_{h} inner sweeps, where a feedforward step evaluates it once. Standard dropout would draw a fresh mask at every evaluation, so each sweep would relax a different energy and there would be no single equilibrium for the free phase to reach or for the finite difference to compare. We therefore use one mask per sample, held fixed across every sweep and phase of that sample’s training step. It is drawn as standard dropout draws it, so only the redrawing frequency differs, and for the feedforward arms — a single evaluation per step — the two coincide.

sections.heading: FID protocol.
sections.text: All FIDs are computed from 50k samples against the full training set, with EMA weights, and Euler–Heun integration at d ​ t = 0.01 \mathrm{d}t=0.01 . The stopping time τ s \tau_{s} is chosen per model by sampling over a ladder of values and taking the minimum: phase-1 checkpoints are best at the noiseless endpoint τ s = 1 \tau_{s}=1 , and after the contrastive phase the optimum moves well past it (App. I ). The τ s = 3.25 \tau_{s}=3.25 chosen as optimal for the backpropagation arm is also near-optimal for both PCN arms, which a paired sweep of τ s \tau_{s} confirms. For the ImageNet-32 checkpoints we use the authors’ τ s = 2.5 \tau_{s}=2.5 .

sections.heading: Measurement resolution and replication.
sections.text: To gauge the measurement’s resolution we evaluated the backpropagation arm’s phase-1 checkpoint at three sampling seeds: the values span 0.064 0.064 . Changing how the 50k samples are divided across devices moves a fixed-seed evaluation by a similar amount, and unseeded draws of the same checkpoint span 0.15 0.15 . We therefore treat differences below about 0.2 0.2 as unresolved. Our replication reaches 3.54 3.54 after phase 2 where the published model reports 3.34 3.34 ; the authors’ released checkpoint scores 3.44 3.44 under our protocol, so part of the gap is the sampler and part the replication.

sections.heading: Relaxation step sizes.
sections.text: The two blocks take different steps: the errors are updated at d ​ t = 1 \mathrm{d}t=1 , deadbeat up to O ⁡ ( γ ) O(\gamma) for the near-identity Hessian I + γ ​ M I+\gamma M of the error parameterisation (App. E ), while the visible variables take d ​ t x \mathrm{d}t_{x} , whose block carries the spring and the O ⁡ ( γ ) O(\gamma) curvature of E PCN E_{\rm PCN} in x x . Phase 1 uses d ​ t x = 1 \mathrm{d}t_{x}=1 ; phase 2 uses d ​ t x = 0.5 \mathrm{d}t_{x}=0.5 , paired with λ = 2 \lambda=2 so that λ ​ d ​ t x = 1 \lambda\,\mathrm{d}t_{x}=1 (below).

sections.heading: The contrastive phase.
sections.text: The contrastive settings are those of Balcerak et al. (2025) : 200 200 Langevin steps at d ​ t = 0.01 \mathrm{d}t=0.01 and ϵ max = 0.01 \epsilon_{\max}=0.01 , half the chains initialised from data and half from noise on the same noise schedule, entering the loss with weight λ CD = 10 − 3 \lambda_{\rm CD}=10^{-3} as a trimmed mean over the negatives with the top 10 % 10\% dropped and the term clamped at 0.02 0.02 . For the PCN arms, negatives are drawn by a Langevin chain on a feedforward copy of the network carrying the PCN’s current weights, rather than by relaxation, which our compute budget did not extend to; no parameter gradient passes through that copy, and Section 4.1 shows the two velocity fields agree to a cosine similarity of 1 1 to nine decimal places. sections.heading: Appendix K Scope of the claims
sections.text: This appendix states, in one place, what the paper does and does not claim, on four points where a reader might reasonably read more into the results than the evidence supports.

sections.heading: The solver is not the substrate.
sections.text: Every equilibrium in this paper was found by gradient descent in error coordinates (App. E ), and a single deadbeat sweep of that solver is algebraically a backward pass ( Goemaere et al., 2026 , Thm. C.9) . That is a choice of simulation method: the claim of Section 3.1 is a property of the equilibrium, not of the route to it. The local state dynamics equation 36 share that equilibrium exactly and converge towards it (App. E ), but too slowly under explicit discretisation to run at this scale. What the paper establishes is that a state whose local errors carry − ∇ x V -\nabla_{x}V exists, that the parameter updates EP reads from it match backpropagation’s, and that training on those updates works at CIFAR-10 scale. What it does not establish is that a physical system settles there in useful time; that is the open question a substrate would answer.

sections.heading: What is new.
sections.text: The paper builds on known ingredients: that a PCN’s equilibrium errors implement the backward pass ( Whittington and Bogacz, 2017 ; Millidge et al., 2022 ) , the spring-clamped free phase of GradEP ( Gower, 2026 ) , and the linearised nudge of Dual Propagation ( Høier et al., 2023 ) . Its contributions are the injection-term construction that turns a scalar-output network into one whose visible layer carries − ∇ x V -\nabla_{x}V (Proposition 1 ); the joint γ \gamma – β \beta window and its derivation (App. C , Table 3 ); and the demonstration that these compose into competitive generation on CIFAR-10, where prior backpropagation-free generative models remain at MNIST scale.

sections.heading: Where a backward pass remains in training.
sections.text: The EP arm’s parameter updates in both phases come from measurements at equilibrium. Its phase-2 negatives, however, were sampled by a feedforward twin of the network using autograd velocities, since relaxing 200 200 Langevin steps per negative was beyond our budget. No parameter gradient passes through the twin, and the two velocity fields agree to a cosine similarity of 1 1 to nine decimal places (Section 4.1 ), so we expect replacing it with relaxation changes the negatives by an amount below the sampler’s own noise, though we did not test this. “Without backpropagation” in Section 5 refers to how the weights were updated, not to every computation the training loop performed.

sections.heading: The hardware-plausible architecture is an existence proof.
sections.text: The norm- and attention-free network of Section 5.1 is wider than the reference, used a different schedule, and was trained and sampled feedforward only. Its FID of 3.51 3.51 shows that neither component is needed for competitive generation; it does not show that they can be removed at matched cost, nor that the resulting network trains under EP. Both are left to future work, as is the run-to-run variance of every arm in Table 2 , each of which is a single run.

sections.heading: Appendix L Generated samples
sections.text: Figures 8 – 11 show 128 128 samples from each of the four trained models of Section 5 , drawn from each model’s phase-2 checkpoint under its own native inference — feedforward autograd for the two backpropagation-trained models, PCN relaxation for the other two. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential — but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths.
